q: When must Flight Attendants verify the suitability of exit seat customers?
a: Prior to each door closure, to ensure each customer meets exit seat criteria.

src.quote: must verify suitability of exit seat customers prior to each door closure
src.note: Verification is repeated before every door closure, not just at initial boarding, so re-boarded or reseated passengers are re-checked.

q: Who has final authority in determining suitability of exit seat occupants?
a: The Flight Attendants, in accordance with FAA regulations.

src.quote: Flight Attendants have final authority in determining suitability criteria of exit seat occupants on board the aircraft
src.note: A CRO may be consulted for an exit seat disability concern, but the FA retains final say on exit-seat suitability.

q: If a CRO does not deny boarding, can the PIC still override that decision?
a: Yes. The PIC has authority to override the CRO's decision based on a safety-of-flight concern.

src.quote: If a CRO does not deny boarding, the PIC has the authority to override the decision based on a safety-of-flight concern.
src.note: The CRO manages ACAA compliance, but safety of flight keeps the PIC as the final decision-maker on carriage.

q: When ACAA compliance conflicts with an FAA regulation, which takes precedence?

src.quote: if ACAA compliance conflicts with FAA regulation, FAA regulations take precedence
src.note: A CRO may waive Company policy to mitigate a disability, but cannot waive an FAA regulation.

q: How does the FOM define a service animal?
a: A dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a qualified individual with a disability.

src.quote: A service animal is defined as a dog, regardless of breed or type, that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks
src.note: The disability covered may be physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.

q: After an in-flight unacceptable service animal incident, what should the Flight Crew relay?
a: Seat number, passenger name, a brief description of the incident, and a request that a CRO meet the aircraft.

src.quote: Request that a CRO meet the aircraft
src.note: At the gate the FAs instead consult a CRO before departure per 13.3.1; the four-item relay applies after departure.

q: May spare lithium batteries be placed in checked baggage?
a: No. Spare lithium batteries may not be placed in checked baggage due to the potential fire hazard; they must go in carry-on baggage.

src.quote: Spare lithium batteries of any type, including external battery chargers containing a lithium-ion battery, may not be placed in checked baggage because of the potential fire hazard
src.note: Checked baggage may only contain lithium batteries installed in a device; spares must be carried on with terminals covered/insulated.

q: When may passengers use cell phone transmit (talk/text) features during a ground delay?
a: During a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer, with the Captain's permission.

src.quote: during a ground delay of 15 minutes or longer with the Captain's permission
src.note: Transmit features are also allowed until door closure and while taxiing to the gate on arrival; the Captain may suspend use at any time if interference is suspected.

q: Which mobility-device batteries may be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin?
a: Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices; all other mobility device batteries must be stowed in the cargo compartment.

src.quote: Only lithium-ion batteries used to power mobility devices can be carried and stowed in the passenger cabin.
src.note: A NOTOC is not required for these batteries; wet-cell (spillable) and gel/dry-cell batteries go in the cargo compartment.

q: What will the Flight Deck Report state when a lithium-ion wheelchair battery is carried in the cabin?
a: The Flight Deck Report will state "Lithium Battery Wheelchair," and the "A" FA/FFA notifies the Captain of the battery's location.

src.quote: the Flight Deck Report will state “Lithium Battery Wheelchair.”
src.note: Wheelchairs with lithium-ion batteries that cannot be easily removed will not be transported; the removed battery rides in the cabin.

q: Are Portable Oxygen Concentrators (POCs) considered HAZMAT?
a: No. Authorized POCs are not considered HAZMAT and may be carried in the cabin and used by passengers.

src.note: An authorized POC is on the FAA-approved list or bears a red-lettered label stating it meets FAA-acceptance criteria.

q: How must filled oxygen bottles be transported, and what documents are required?
a: In an approved container (superbox), shipped as HAZMAT; a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required.

src.quote: filled oxygen bottles must be transported in an approved container (superbox) and are shipped as HAZMAT; therefore, a NOTOC and the Emergency Response Guide (ERG) are required
src.note: Empty oxygen bottles are not HAZMAT and require no superbox or NOTOC; a DOT Special Permit allows filled bottles without a superbox within Alaska to remote communities.

q: How does the crew handle a DNR request to withhold resuscitation on board?
a: Cabin crews are obligated to perform resuscitation attempts; any request to withhold must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink.

src.quote: any request to withhold resuscitation attempts must be denied unless otherwise instructed by MedLink
src.note: Alaska cannot validate a DNR order in flight, but will not refuse travel to a DNR customer if escort/other requirements are met.

q: In an apparent death on board, until when is the individual presumed alive?
a: The individual is presumed alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred.

src.quote: The individual is presumed to be alive until MedLink or a physician has determined that death has occurred.
src.note: MedLink assumes liability for stopping CPR; radio communication to indicate a death occurred on board is inappropriate.

q: Under the Fallen Soldier Program, how are the family and military escort boarded and deplaned?
a: "Last On" during boarding and "First Off" during deplaning; the military escort is seated in first class if available.

src.quote: The family and military escort should be “Last On” during boarding and “First Off” during deplaning.
src.note: The remains normally load into an aft pit; keep the Seat Belt Sign illuminated until after the escort and family have deplaned (13.14.3.2).
